topics.title: Arrays & Hashing

card.summary: Return true if any value appears at least twice in an array.
card.clue: 'Appears twice' = 'have I seen this before?'
card.trick: Add each number to a set; if it's already there, return true.

card.summary: Decide whether two strings use exactly the same letters the same number of times.
card.clue: 'Same letters, same counts' = frequency counting.
card.trick: Count letters in both strings and compare the counts (or one counter: +1 for s, −1 for t).

card.summary: Return the indexes of the two numbers in an unsorted array that add up to a target.
card.clue: A pair that sums to a target, unsorted, and you need the original indexes.
card.trick: For each x, look up target − x in a map of values already seen.

card.summary: Group a list of words so that words made of the same letters end up together.
card.technique: Hash map with a signature key
card.clue: 'Group things that are the same in some way' = one key per group.
card.trick: Key each word by its sorted letters (or a 26-count tuple); words with the same key go in the same list.

card.summary: Return the k numbers that appear most often.
card.clue: 'K most frequent' = count, then pick the top k.
card.trick: Count with a map, then put numbers into buckets indexed by count and read from the highest bucket: O(n).

card.summary: Turn a list of strings into one string and back again, even if the strings contain any characters.
card.clue: Any character can appear, so you can't rely on a separator alone.
card.trick: Write each string as length + '#' + string; when decoding, read the number up to '#', then take exactly that many characters.

card.summary: For every index, return the product of all the other numbers, without using division.
card.clue: 'Everything except me' without division = everything left of me × everything right of me.
card.trick: One pass left-to-right stores the product before each index; a second pass right-to-left multiplies in the product after it.

card.summary: Check whether a partly filled 9 × 9 Sudoku board breaks any rule so far.
card.technique: Hash sets per row, column and box
card.clue: 'No repeats in each row, column and 3 × 3 box' = seen-before checks in three groups.
card.trick: Keep a set for every row, column and box; the box index is (r // 3, c // 3).

card.summary: Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (in any order) in O(n).
card.technique: Hash set, start only at sequence starts
card.clue: O(n) required, and order in the array doesn't matter.
card.trick: Put all numbers in a set; only count upwards from n when n − 1 is missing.

content.title: Arrays & Hashing
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Arrays & Hashing.
content.whatItIs: Think of Arrays and Hashing as your foundation. An array is just a contiguous block of memory where you store items in a row, like parking spots in a lot. Hashing (using a HashMap or HashSet) is a magical tool that lets you answer the question 'Have I seen this before?' or 'Where is this item?' in exactly 1 step (O(1) time). When you combine them, you get the absolute best of both worlds: checking if things exist instantly, while keeping track of all items.
whenToUse: When you need to count how many times an element appears.
When you need to look up an element instantly O(1) without looping through the array again.
When you need to map a specific key to a specific value.
When the problem asks for pairs, duplicates, or missing numbers.
content.howItWorks: Usually, you loop through an array from left to right. As you look at each item, you ask your Hash Map a question (e.g., 'Have I seen your pair before?'). If the answer is yes, you're done! If no, you simply throw that current item into the Hash Map and move on to the next one.

steps: Look at 2. Ask Map: Do you have 9-2 (7)? Map says no. Add 2 to Map.
Look at 7. Ask Map: Do you have 9-7 (2)? Map says YES! We found our pair.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that Hash Maps use more memory (Space Complexity becomes O(N)).
Trying to use Arrays for lookups instead of HashSets, which makes your code O(N^2) instead of O(N).

interviewTips.whatToSay: 'I can immediately optimize the O(N^2) brute force solution to O(N) by trading space for time using a HashMap.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: Be ready to explain how Hash Collisions work.

relatedPatterns.description: Often combined with HashMaps to remember running totals.

guide.hook: Seen it before? Ask the hash map — one step, not a second loop.
guide.idea: A hash map (dict) or hash set answers 'have I seen this?' or 'where is it?' in one step. Instead of a nested loop that compares every pair, you walk the array once and remember what you've seen.
guide.analogy: A cloakroom. You hand over your coat and get ticket 47. Later, ticket 47 takes the attendant straight to your coat — no searching every hook.
guide.breaks: A real cloakroom can run out of hooks. A hash map just grows, but it costs memory: you trade O(n) extra space for speed.
signals: 'Find a pair / two numbers that…' in an unsorted array
'Duplicate', 'seen before', 'unique', 'missing'
'Count how many times' or 'most frequent'
'Group things that are the same in some way' (anagrams)
You catch yourself writing a nested loop to look something up

lookAlikes.clue: If the array is sorted (or you may sort it) and they want O(1) extra space, walk two pointers instead of storing a map.
If you need the items in order, or the k-th position, sort. If you only need 'does it exist / how many', hash it.

guide.gutCheck: Am I looking something up again and again? → put it in a hash map.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR X["next item x"] --> Q{"is what x needs
already in the map?"} Q -->|"yes"| A["answer found ✓"] Q -->|"no"| S["store x in the map"] --> X
diagram.caption: One pass. Each item first asks the map, then joins it.

guide.template:
def solve(nums):
    seen = {}                      # value -> what you need to remember (index, count…)
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = ...                 # what x is looking for (e.g. target - x)
        if need in seen:           # O(1) lookup instead of a second loop
            return ...             # found the answer
        seen[x] = i                # remember x AFTER checking, so x can't pair with itself
    return ...                     # nothing found
mistakes: Storing the item before checking for its pair, so an item pairs with itself (Two Sum with 3 + 3 = 6 on [3]).
Using a list for 'in' checks: x in list is O(n), x in set is O(1).
Forgetting a dict key must be hashable: use a tuple, not a list, as a key (Group Anagrams).

easy.title: Two Sum
easy.insight: Checking before storing means each number only meets numbers that came before it — every pair is still found exactly once.

medium.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
medium.insight: Only start counting at a sequence's first number (where n − 1 is missing). That keeps the whole thing O(n), even with the inner while loop.

topics.title: Two Pointers

card.summary: Decide whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case and non-letters.
card.clue: 'Palindrome' = compare the two ends moving inwards.
card.trick: Skip non-alphanumeric characters with each pointer, compare lower-case letters, move both inwards.

problems.title: Two Sum II Input Array Is Sorted

card.summary: In a sorted array, find the two numbers that add up to a target, using constant extra space.
card.clue: Sorted + a pair + O(1) space.
card.trick: Sum too small → move the left pointer right; too big → move the right pointer left.

card.summary: Find all unique triplets that add up to zero.
card.clue: A triplet sum is a pair sum (Two Sum II) for every fixed first number.
card.trick: Sort; for each i, run two pointers on the rest for −nums[i]; skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triplets.

card.summary: Pick two vertical lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water.
card.technique: Two pointers, move the shorter wall
card.clue: Two walls limit each other: area = shorter height × distance.
card.trick: Start at both ends and always move the shorter wall; moving the taller one can never help.

card.summary: Given bar heights, compute how much rain water is trapped between them.
card.technique: Two pointers with left max and right max
card.clue: Water above a bar depends on the tallest bar on each side.
card.trick: Water at i = min(max left, max right) − height[i]; move the side with the smaller max, since that side is the limit.

content.title: Two Pointers
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Two Pointers.
content.whatItIs: Imagine you and a friend are searching a library. Instead of you searching the whole library alone, you start at the front door, and your friend starts at the back door. You walk towards each other until you meet in the middle. That's the Two Pointer technique! It's a strategy where you use two variables (pointers) to iterate through an array or string simultaneously, usually from opposite ends or moving at different speeds.
whenToUse: When dealing with sorted arrays or string palindromes.
When searching for pairs that sum up to a target (if sorted).
When reversing an array or string completely in-place.
content.howItWorks: You initialize a `left` pointer at index 0, and a `right` pointer at the last index. You run a `while (left < right)` loop. Depending on the condition, you either move the left pointer forward `left++` or the right pointer backward `right--` until they meet.

steps: left='r', right='r'. They match. Move pointers inward (left++, right--).
left='a', right='a'. They match. Move inward.
left='c', right='c'. They match.
left and right cross paths at 'e'. It's a valid Palindrome!

commonMistakes: Using a `while (left <= right)` loop when it should technically be `left < right` (which might cause double inner swaps).
Forgetting to actually increment or decrement the pointers inside the loop, causing an infinite loop crash!

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The array is explicitly SORTED, or you need to find a combination of elements at opposite ends.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Since the array is sorted, we can avoid O(N) extra space by using two pointers from opposite ends.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: What if there are duplicates in the sorted array? (You might have to skip them).

relatedPatterns.description: A variation of Two Pointers where the pointers move in the same direction.

medium.title: Two Sum II Input Array Is Sorted

guide.hook: Sorted? Start at both ends and walk inwards — each move throws away an impossible answer.
guide.idea: Two indexes move through the data at the same time, usually one from each end. Each comparison tells you which pointer can move, so you rule out many answers per step and finish in one pass.
guide.analogy: Finding two friends whose heights add to 3 metres in a line sorted by height. Too short in total? Swap the shortest for the next one up. Too tall? Swap the tallest for the next one down.
guide.breaks: With friends you could just look around. The trick only works because the order is known: moving a pointer is safe only when sorting guarantees everything you skip is worse.
signals: The input is sorted (or sorting it is allowed)
'Pair / triplet that sums to…' in a sorted array
'Palindrome', 'reverse in place'
'Container', 'trapping water' — two walls that limit each other
They ask for O(1) extra space

lookAlikes.clue: Window = a contiguous range where both pointers move the same way. Two pointers here = opposite ends moving towards each other.
Unsorted and you can't sort (you need original indexes)? Use a hash map instead.

guide.gutCheck: Sorted, and I'm comparing a pair from both ends? → two pointers.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  L["L →"] --- A["sorted array"] --- R["← R"]
  A --> Q{"compare arr[L] and arr[R]"}
  Q -->|"too small"| ML["move L right"]
  Q -->|"too big"| MR["move R left"]
  Q -->|"just right"| D["answer ✓"]
diagram.caption: Every comparison lets one pointer move, ruling out answers that can't work.

guide.template:
def solve(arr):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        if ...:            # found what you want
            return ...
        elif ...:          # left side too small / worse
            left += 1
        else:              # right side too big / worse
            right -= 1
    return ...
guide.time: O(n) (O(n log n) if you must sort first)
mistakes: Using left <= right when the two pointers must be different items (it should be left < right).
In 3Sum, not skipping repeated values, so the same triplet appears twice.
Moving the wrong pointer in Container With Most Water: always move the shorter wall, because the taller one can't help while the shorter one limits the height.

easy.title: Two Sum II (sorted input)
easy.insight: When the sum is too big, L already holds the smallest number left, so R is too big with every partner. R can never be in the answer — move it.

medium.title: Container With Most Water
medium.insight: The shorter wall decides the height. Moving the taller wall can only shrink the width without raising the height, so always move the shorter one.

mistakes: Using left <= right when the two pointers must be different items (it should be left < right).
In 3Sum, not skipping repeated values, so the same triplet appears twice.
Moving the wrong pointer in Container With Most Water: always move the shorter wall, because the taller one can't help while the shorter one limits the height.
Forgetting to actually increment or decrement the pointers inside the loop, causing an infinite loop crash!

topics.title: Sliding Window

problems.title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock

card.summary: Pick one day to buy and a later day to sell for the biggest profit.
card.clue: Buy before sell, best difference across the array.
card.trick: Keep the cheapest price so far as the left edge; profit = today − cheapest.

card.summary: Find the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.
card.clue: 'Longest substring such that …' = contiguous range with a rule.
card.trick: Expand right; while the new character is already in the window, remove from the left.

card.summary: With at most k letter changes, find the longest substring of one repeated letter.
card.clue: 'Longest substring' with 'at most k' changes.
card.trick: A window is valid while (window length − count of its most common letter) ≤ k; shrink when it's not.

card.summary: Decide whether some rearrangement of string s1 appears as a substring of s2.
card.clue: A rearrangement has the same length and the same letter counts.
card.trick: Slide a window of length len(s1) over s2, updating letter counts, and compare with s1's counts.

card.summary: Find the shortest substring of s containing every character of t (with counts).
card.clue: 'Shortest substring containing all of …'.
card.trick: Expand until all needed counts are met, then shrink from the left while still valid, recording the shortest.

card.summary: Return the maximum of every window of size k.
card.clue: Fixed window size, and you need the max each time.
card.trick: Keep a deque of indexes with decreasing values; drop the front when it leaves the window — the front is the max.

content.title: Sliding Window
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Sliding Window.
content.whatItIs: Think of a Sliding Window as taking a rectangular frame and dragging it across a long picture. Instead of examining the entire picture at once, you only process what fits inside your frame at any given exact moment. As the frame slides to the right, one new item comes into view, and one old item drops out. This is incredibly powerful for analyzing sub-arrays.
whenToUse: When asked to find the longest/shortest 'substring' or 'subarray'.
When looking for a continuous sequence that meets a certain condition.
When finding the max/min sum of a specific window size 'K'.
content.howItWorks: You use two forward-moving pointers, `left` and `right`. The `right` pointer expands the window by moving forward in the loop. If the window ever becomes invalid (e.g., getting too large or containing duplicates), you smoothly shrink it by moving the `left` pointer forward until it's valid again.

steps: Right='a'. Window='a'. Max=1.
Right='b'. Window='ab'. Max=2.
Right='c'. Window='abc'. Max=3.
Right='a' (duplicate detected!). Shrink left to drop the old 'a'. Window='bca'. Max=3.

commonMistakes: Growing the right pointer before shrinking the left pointer correctly.
Using O(N^2) nested loops when a sliding window makes it beautiful O(N).
Off-by-one errors when calculating the mathematical window size using `right - left + 1`.

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The prompt explicitly uses the words 'contiguous', 'substring', 'subarray', or 'window'.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Since we need a contiguous subarray, we can maintain a sliding window to keep our time complexity strictly linear.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: Can you do this if the array has negative numbers? (Hint: usually sliding window fails for sums with negatives, use prefix arrays instead).

relatedPatterns.description: Sliding window literally uses two pointers, just constrained differently.

easy.title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock

guide.hook: Grow the right edge; while the window breaks the rule, shrink the left edge.
guide.idea: A window is a contiguous slice [left, right]. You extend it to the right one step at a time, and whenever it stops being valid you move the left edge forward until it's valid again. Each item enters and leaves the window at most once, so it's O(n).
guide.analogy: Reading a long sentence through a cardboard slot you can stretch. You widen it to see more words; when it shows something you're not allowed (a repeated letter), you slide the left edge until it's gone.
guide.breaks: A cardboard slot can jump anywhere. The window can't: both edges only ever move right, which is exactly what makes it O(n).
signals: 'Contiguous subarray' or 'substring'
'Longest / shortest / maximum … such that …'
'At most k', 'without repeating', 'containing all of'
A fixed size: 'every window of size k'

lookAlikes.clue: Both use left and right. Sliding window keeps everything between them (a contiguous range) and both move the same way.
'Subarray sum equals k' with negative numbers: shrinking the window doesn't reliably reduce the sum, so the window breaks — use prefix sums.

guide.gutCheck: Contiguous range, and I want the best one that obeys a rule? → sliding window.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["move right one step:
add the new item"] --> Q{"window breaks
the rule?"} Q -->|"yes"| S["remove the left item,
move left one step"] --> Q Q -->|"no"| U["update the best answer"] --> A
diagram.caption: Expand, shrink while invalid, record. Both edges only move right.

guide.template:
def solve(s):
    left = 0
    state = ...                         # what's inside the window (set, counts, sum)
    best = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        # 1. add s[right] to the window
        while ...:                      # 2. while the window breaks the rule
            # remove s[left] from the window
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)   # 3. window is valid: record it
    return best
guide.space: O(k) for what's inside the window (often a set or counts)
mistakes: Using if instead of while to shrink: one step may not be enough to make the window valid again.
Updating the best answer before the window is valid.
Window length is right − left + 1, not right − left.

easy.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
easy.insight: If today's price is lower than the buy price, no future sale would rather use the old buy day — so jump the left edge here.

medium.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
medium.insight: When a letter repeats, the window must drop everything up to and including the earlier copy — that's the while loop.
medium.code:
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = set()
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        while ch in seen:              # shrink until ch is no longer repeated
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(ch)
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

mistakes: Using if instead of while to shrink: one step may not be enough to make the window valid again.
Updating the best answer before the window is valid.
Window length is right − left + 1, not right − left.
Growing the right pointer before shrinking the left pointer correctly.
Using O(N^2) nested loops when a sliding window makes it beautiful O(N).

topics.title: Stack

card.summary: Decide whether a string of brackets is correctly opened and closed.
card.clue: Nested matching pairs.
card.trick: Push openers; each closer must match the top of the stack; the stack must end empty.

card.summary: Design a stack that also returns its minimum in O(1).
card.technique: Stack with a second 'minimum so far' stack
card.clue: O(1) minimum while items come and go in stack order.
card.trick: Alongside each pushed value, push the minimum so far; popping removes both.

card.summary: Evaluate an expression written in reverse Polish notation, like ['2', '1', '+', '3', '*'].
card.clue: Each operator uses the two most recent numbers.
card.trick: Push numbers; on an operator, pop two (b first, then a), push a op b; divide truncating towards zero.

card.summary: For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature?
card.clue: 'How long until the next greater…'.
card.trick: Keep waiting days on a stack; a warmer day pops and answers all cooler days on top.

card.summary: Cars drive towards a target at different speeds and can't overtake; count how many fleets arrive.
card.clue: Cars can't pass, so a faster car behind joins the one ahead.
card.trick: Sort by position from closest to the target; compute arrival times; a car that would arrive sooner than the fleet ahead merges into it.

card.summary: Find the largest rectangle that fits inside a histogram.
card.clue: For each bar: how far can it stretch left and right before a shorter bar?
card.trick: Keep increasing heights on a stack; when a shorter bar arrives, pop and compute each popped bar's widest rectangle.

content.title: Stack
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Stack.
content.whatItIs: Imagine a stack of dinner plates. You can only put a new plate on the very top, and when you need a plate, you can only grab the one from the very top. You can't magically pull one from the middle! This is a Stack data structure. It operates strictly on the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle. Whatever goes in last is the absolute first thing that comes out.
whenToUse: When you need to remember previous states and return to them in reverse order.
When parsing brackets, tags, or mathematical expressions (like `([{ }])`).
When dealing with 'Next Greater Element' or 'Previous Smaller Element' problems.
When implementing Undo features or browsing history.
content.howItWorks: You create a Stack (often just a dynamic array or built-in Stack class). You `push()` elements onto the top of the stack as you process them. When you need to backtrack or match a previous element, you `pop()` from the top. You can also `peek()` to just look at the top element without removing it.

steps: See '('. It's an opening bracket, push to stack.
See ')'. It's closing. Does it match the top of the stack '('? Yes! Pop it.
See '['. Push.
See ']'. Matches top. Pop.
See '{'. Push.
See '}'. Matches top. Pop. Stack is empty, so it's valid!

commonMistakes: Forgetting to check if the stack `isEmpty()` before calling `.pop()` or `.peek()`, causing a sudden crash.
Leaving elements in the stack at the end and mistakenly assuming the string is valid without checking `return stack.isEmpty()`.

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The problem involves 'matching' elements, 'nearest', 'undo', or checking if things are 'validly nested'.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Because we need to evaluate the most recently seen items first, I'll use a Stack to enforce Last-In-First-Out processing.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: How would you implement a Stack using only Queues?

relatedPatterns.description: A special stack where elements are forced to be entirely increasing or decreasing. Extremely useful for 'Next Greater Element' problems.

guide.hook: The most recent unfinished thing comes first: push it, and pop when its match arrives.
guide.idea: A stack is last-in, first-out. Use it when the newest item is the one that gets resolved next: matching brackets, undo, or 'the next greater element' (a monotonic stack keeps items in sorted order and pops everything the new item beats).
guide.analogy: A pile of plates: you add and remove only from the top. For brackets, every closing one must match the plate on top.
guide.breaks: Plates don't care about order. A monotonic stack does: before pushing, it pops every item smaller (or bigger) than the new one, and that pop is the moment you record an answer.
signals: 'Valid parentheses', nested or matching pairs
'Next greater / smaller element', 'how many days until warmer'
'Evaluate an expression', 'decode a string'
'Undo', 'backspace', 'most recent'

lookAlikes.clue: First-in, first-out (process in arrival order, level by level) → queue. Most recent first → stack.
A palindrome check uses two pointers; nested matching (brackets) needs a stack because pairs can wrap around each other.

guide.gutCheck: Does the newest item get resolved first, or do I need the next bigger thing? → stack.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR N["next value x"] --> Q{"stack not empty and
top value < x?"} Q -->|"yes"| P["pop the top:
its answer is x"] --> Q Q -->|"no"| PU["push x"] --> N
diagram.caption: A monotonic stack: everything x beats is popped and answered; then x waits on the stack for its own answer.

guide.time: O(n): each item is pushed and popped at most once
mistakes: Popping from an empty stack: check if stack before stack[-1].
Forgetting the leftovers at the end: in Valid Parentheses, a non-empty stack means unmatched openers.
Storing values when you need distances: push indexes, then i − j gives the gap (Daily Temperatures).

easy.title: Valid Parentheses
easy.insight: A closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opener — exactly what the top of the stack is.

medium.title: Daily Temperatures
medium.insight: Days wait on the stack until a warmer day arrives. Each day is pushed once and popped once, so it's O(n), not O(n²).

mistakes: Popping from an empty stack: check if stack before stack[-1].
Forgetting the leftovers at the end: in Valid Parentheses, a non-empty stack means unmatched openers.
Storing values when you need distances: push indexes, then i − j gives the gap (Daily Temperatures).

topics.title: Binary Search

card.summary: Find a target's index in a sorted array in O(log n).
card.clue: Sorted + O(log n).
card.trick: Check the middle and discard the half that can't contain the target.

card.summary: Search a matrix whose rows are sorted and each row starts after the previous one ends.
card.technique: Binary search on a flattened index
card.clue: The whole matrix is one sorted list in disguise.
card.trick: Binary search index 0 … m·n − 1, mapping mid to row mid // n and column mid % n.

card.summary: Find the slowest eating speed that finishes all banana piles within h hours.
card.clue: 'Minimum speed such that …' — slow speeds fail, fast speeds pass.
card.trick: Search speeds 1 … max(piles); hours = sum of ceil(pile / k); keep the smallest speed that fits.

problems.title: Find Minimum In Rotated Sorted Array

card.summary: Find the smallest number in a sorted array that has been rotated.
card.technique: Binary search comparing with the right end
card.clue: Sorted but rotated, O(log n).
card.trick: If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum is right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to its left.

card.summary: Find a target in a rotated sorted array in O(log n).
card.technique: Binary search, find the sorted half
card.clue: Sorted but rotated, O(log n).
card.trick: One half around mid is always sorted; check whether the target lies inside that half to decide where to go.

card.summary: Store values with timestamps and return the latest value at or before a given time.
card.technique: Hash map + binary search on timestamps
card.clue: Timestamps arrive in increasing order, and you need 'the last one ≤ t'.
card.trick: Map each key to a list of (time, value); binary search for the rightmost time ≤ t.

card.summary: Find the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(m + n)).
card.clue: Two sorted arrays and a log-time requirement.
card.trick: Binary search how many items to take from the smaller array so that the left halves together hold half the items and every left item ≤ every right item.

content.title: Binary Search
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Binary Search.
content.whatItIs: If you're looking for the word 'Elephant' in a physical dictionary, you don't start at page 1 and read every single word. You open the book to the exact middle. If you see 'Monkey', you know 'Elephant' must be in the left half, so you rip the book in half and throw away the right side. You repeat this until you find it! Binary Search is the algorithmic version of this: it dramatically cuts the search space in half with every single step.
whenToUse: When the array is ALREADY SORTED.
When the problem asks for an O(log N) runtime explicitly.
When you are searching for a specific target value or condition.
When the problem involves a continuous range of numbers (e.g., 'find the minimum capacity').
content.howItWorks: You set `left = 0` and `right = array.length - 1`. You enter a loop `while (left <= right)`. You calculate the exact middle index (`mid = left + (right - left) / 2`). If `array[mid]` is exactly what you want, you win! If `array[mid]` is too small, you search the right half (`left = mid + 1`). If it's too big, you search the left half (`right = mid - 1`).

steps: left=0, right=5. mid=2 (nums[2] is 3). 3 is less than 9. Throw away left half. left=3.
left=3, right=5. mid=4 (nums[4] is 9). 9 equals target! We found it at index 4.

commonMistakes: Calculating mid as `(left + right) / 2`, which can cause a serious integer overflow if the array is massive. Always use `left + (right - left) / 2`.
Messing up the `<` vs `<=` in the while loop condition.
Forgetting to add/subtract 1 (`left = mid + 1`) and causing an infinite loop.

guide.hook: Sorted, or 'yes, yes, yes, no, no'? Check the middle and throw half away.
guide.idea: If you can ask a yes/no question whose answers flip only once across a range (sorted values, or 'is speed k fast enough?'), test the middle and discard the half that can't contain the answer. Each step halves the range: O(log n).
guide.analogy: Guessing a number from 1 to 100 with 'higher or lower' hints. Always guess the middle and you need at most 7 guesses.
guide.breaks: The guessing game always has a number. Binary search on the answer needs a range of possible answers and a check that flips exactly once — you have to design that check yourself.
signals: Sorted array or matrix; 'O(log n)' required
'Minimum speed / capacity / time such that …' (search on the answer)
'Rotated sorted array'
'Find the first / last position where …'

If checking one candidate answer is easy but the answer range is huge, binary search the answer instead of trying them all.

guide.gutCheck: Can I ask 'is the answer ≤ mid?' and get yes/no that flips once? → binary search.

flowchart LR R["range lo … hi"] --> M["mid = (lo + hi) // 2"] M --> Q{"does mid work?"} Q -->|"yes"| H["keep the left half
hi = mid"] Q -->|"no"| L["keep the right half
lo = mid + 1"] H & L --> C{"lo == hi?"} C -->|"no"| M C -->|"yes"| A["answer = lo"]

guide.template:
def binary_search_on_answer(lo, hi):
    # find the smallest value in [lo, hi] for which ok(value) is True
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid):        # mid works -> the answer is mid or smaller
            hi = mid
        else:              # mid fails -> the answer is bigger
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def ok(value):
    ...                    # your yes/no check
guide.time: O(log n), or O(n log(range)) when each check costs O(n)
mistakes: Infinite loops: with while lo < hi, set hi = mid (not mid − 1) and lo = mid + 1.
Using lo <= hi with hi = mid, which loops forever when lo == hi.
Searching the answer space without checking the check really flips only once.

content.title: Linked List
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Linked List.
content.whatItIs: Imagine you are following a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where to find the next one. Each clue card has two parts: the message on it (the data) and the directions to the next clue (the pointer). A linked list works in the same way: every node stores some data and a reference that leads you to the next node in the chain. If you want to reach the 5th clue, you cannot teleport to it; you must start at the first card and follow the trail one clue at a time. Linked lists behave like that too: to reach the 5th node, you begin at the head and move through each node in order, unlike an array where you can directly jump to any element using its index.
whenToUse: When you need fast O(1) insertions or deletions at the ends.
When you do NOT need random access (like `array[5]`).
When building Stacks, Queues, or LRU Caches.
content.howItWorks: You always start by holding the `head` node. To traverse the list, you use a loop: `while(curr != null)` and simply jump to the next item via `curr = curr.next;`. When modifying the list (like insertions/deletions), you carefully rearrange the `.next` pointers before deleting anything so you don't lose the rest of the chain!

steps: Node 1: Point next to null. Prev=1, Curr=2
Node 2: Point next to 1. Prev=2, Curr=3
Node 3: Point next to 2. Prev=3, Curr=null
Curr is null, loop ends. New head is 3! Return [3,2,1]

commonMistakes: Losing the reference to the rest of the list! Always save `curr.next` into a temporary variable before mutating `curr`.
Null Pointer Exceptions. You must constantly check `if (curr != null && curr.next != null)` before accessing properties.
Forgetting to handle edge cases like empty lists (`head == null`).

guide.analogy: A treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is. To reverse the hunt, you rewrite each clue to point back — but read where it pointed before you overwrite it.
guide.breaks: Treasure-hunt clues stay in place. In code, once you overwrite node.next without saving it, the rest of the list is lost for good.

'Reverse', 'reorder', 'merge', 'remove the n-th node from the end'
'Cycle', 'middle of the list'
'O(1) extra space' with a list

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Before
    A1["1"] --> A2["2"] --> A3["3"] --> N1["None"]
  end
  subgraph After
    B3["3"] --> B2["2"] --> B1["1"] --> N2["None"]
  end

guide.template:
def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next          # 1. save what comes next
        curr.next = prev         # 2. point backwards
        prev, curr = curr, nxt   # 3. step forward
    return prev                  # new head

def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:    # fast moves 2, slow moves 1
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    return slow                  # slow is in the middle

mistakes: Losing the rest of the list by changing curr.next before saving it.
Special-casing the head instead of using a dummy node in front of it.
In fast/slow, checking fast.next without first checking fast.

easy.insight: Three variables are all you need: where you came from (prev), where you are (curr), and where you go next (nxt).

def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev, curr = curr, nxt
    return prev

medium.insight: Keep a gap of n + 1 between the pointers. When fast falls off the end, slow is just before the node to remove — in one pass.
medium.code:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    slow = fast = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):        # open a gap of n + 1
        fast = fast.next
    while fast:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next    # skip the n-th from the end
    return dummy.next

Special-casing the head instead of using a dummy node in front of it.

content.title: Trees
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Trees.
content.whatItIs: A Tree is just like a Linked List, but instead of one 'next' pointer, a node can have multiple pointers (like 'left' and 'right'). It branches out exactly like a real tree! The most common type is a Binary Tree, where each node has at most two children. The very top node is called the 'root', and nodes with no children are called 'leaves'. Trees are incredible for representing hierarchical data, like file systems, company org charts, or family trees.
whenToUse: When data is naturally hierarchical.
When you need to perform fast O(log N) searches, insertions, and deletions (using a Binary Search Tree).
When you need to traverse data in a specific order (In-order, Pre-order, Post-order).
content.howItWorks: Because trees are recursive by nature (every child is the 'root' of its own smaller subtree), the most elegant way to work with them is using Recursion! You write a function that does something to the current node, and then simply calls itself on the `left` child and the `right` child. You'll almost always use Depth-First Search (DFS) with recursion, or Breadth-First Search (BFS) using a Queue to go level-by-level.

steps: At root 4: swap left (2) and right (7). Recursively call invert(2) and invert(7).
At 2: swap 1 and 3.
At 7: swap null and null.
All subtrees inverted. The whole tree is now a mirror image!

content.spaceComplexity: O(H) where H is the height of the tree (due to the recursive call stack)
commonMistakes: Forgetting the base case `if (root == null) return null;`, causing a StackOverflow exception.
Not trusting the recursion! Beginners often try to manually track tree depth with complicated loops instead of just letting the call stack do the work.

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The input is a `TreeNode`. The problem asks about 'depth', 'lowest common ancestor', or 'level order'.

guide.hook: Trust the recursion: solve it for the left and right children, then combine at the node.
guide.idea: Most tree problems are depth-first: a function that handles one node by calling itself on the left and right children and combining their answers. Problems about 'levels' or 'the closest' use breadth-first search with a queue instead.
guide.analogy: A manager asking two team leads for their team's number, adding their own, and passing the total up. Nobody needs to see the whole company.
guide.breaks: Real managers can be asked twice. In recursion, the base case (an empty child returns 0, None or True) is what stops it — forget it and you crash.

'Level by level', 'right side view', 'minimum depth' → BFS
'Binary search tree': left < node < right

def dfs(node):
    if not node:                      # base case
        return 0
    left = dfs(node.left)             # trust it: the answer for the left subtree
    right = dfs(node.right)           # and for the right subtree
    return 1 + max(left, right)       # combine at this node

content.title: Heap / Priority Queue
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Heap / Priority Queue.
content.whatItIs: Imagine a VIP line at a club. Normal queues are 'First Come, First Served'. But in a Priority Queue (which is usually built using a Heap), the 'most important' person always gets pulled to the front immediately, no matter when they arrived! A Heap is a magical tree structure where the smallest (Min-Heap) or largest (Max-Heap) element is ALWAYS sitting perfectly at the very top, ready to be grabbed.
whenToUse: When you need to repeatedly find the minimum or maximum element in a dynamically changing dataset.
When a problem asks for the 'Top K' or 'Kth Largest/Smallest' elements.
When implementing advanced algorithms like Dijkstra's Shortest Path.
content.howItWorks: Under the hood, a Heap is just an array disguised as a Binary Tree. When you `add()` a new item, it's placed at the bottom and 'bubbles up' to its correct spot depending on its priority. When you `poll()` (remove) the top item, the bottom item is moved to the top and 'bubbles down'. Both operations take exactly O(log N) time, which is much faster than re-sorting an entire array every time!

steps: Create Min-Heap of size 2.
Insert 3, then 2. Heap=[2, 3].
Insert 1. Heap=[1, 2, 3]. Size > 2, so pop smallest (1). Heap=[2, 3].
Insert 5, pop 2. Heap=[3, 5].
Insert 6, pop 3. Heap=[5, 6].
Insert 4, pop 4. Heap=[5, 6]. Done! Top of heap is 5, which is the 2nd largest!

commonMistakes: Using a Max-Heap to find 'Top K Largest' elements (which forces O(N) space and slower runtime) instead of a Min-Heap of size K.
Forgetting that `PriorityQueue` in Java is a Min-Heap by default, not a Max-Heap!

content.title: Backtracking
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Backtracking.
content.whatItIs: Imagine trying to find your way out of a physical maze. You pick a path, and if you hit a dead end, you physically turn around, walk back to the last intersection, and try a different path. This is Backtracking! It's a brute-force method where you exhaustively try to build a solution piece by piece. The moment you realize your current path is invalid (or you've found a full answer), you 'backtrack' (undo your last step) and try another option.
whenToUse: When a problem asks for ALL valid combinations, permutations, or subsets.
When solving puzzles with specific constraints (like Sudoku or N-Queens).
When the input size is inherently small (N < 20).
content.howItWorks: You write a recursive function. You make a 'choice' (e.g. adding a number to a temporary list). You dive deeper by calling the recursive function. Wait for it to finish. Then, you absolutely must UNDO the choice you just made (remove the number from the list). This resets your state so you can safely try the next choice in the loop!

steps: Start empty [].
Add 1 -> [1]. Recurse.
Add 2 -> [1, 2]. Recurse.
Add 3 -> [1, 2, 3]. Recurse. (Save this solution!)
Backtrack: remove 3 -> [1, 2].
Backtrack: remove 2 -> [1]. Add 3 -> [1, 3]... and so on.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to make a 'Deep Copy' of the temporary list when adding it to the final result (`result.add(new ArrayList<>(current))`). If you just add `current`, your final answer will be full of empty lists because of the undo steps!
Forgetting the undo step Entirely! (`current.remove(...)`).

interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Because we need all combinations, the time complexity will naturally be exponential. I will use backtracking to explore the state-space tree.'

guide.idea: Build a solution one choice at a time. After each choice, explore everything that follows, then undo the choice and try the next one. It walks a tree of decisions; pruning cuts off branches that can't succeed.
guide.analogy: Walking a maze with chalk. At every fork, pick a path; at a dead end, walk back to the last fork, rub out your mark and try the next path.

guide.template:
def backtrack_all(nums):
    results, path = [], []

    def backtrack(start):
        results.append(path[:])          # record a COPY (or only when complete)
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            # (optional) prune: skip choices that can't work
            path.append(nums[i])          # choose
            backtrack(i + 1)              # explore (use i to allow reuse)
            path.pop()                    # un-choose

    backtrack(0)
    return results
mistakes: Appending path instead of path[:] (a copy): every saved answer then changes as path changes.
Forgetting to undo the choice (path.pop()) after exploring.
Getting duplicates: sort first and skip equal neighbours at the same depth (Subsets II, Combination Sum II).

content.title: Tries
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Tries.
content.whatItIs: A Trie (pronounced 'try') is a special kind of tree specifically designed to store strings. Each node in the tree represents a single character. If you follow a path from the root down to a leaf, the characters along the way spell out a complete word! It's the ultimate data structure for Auto-Complete and Spell Checkers.
whenToUse: When you need to store a dictionary of words.
When building Auto-Complete features (e.g., 'Find all words starting with `cat`').
When searching for strings character-by-character.
content.howItWorks: Instead of a standard `left` and `right` pointer, a TrieNode usually holds a HashMap or an array of 26 pointers (one for each letter of the alphabet). You also need a boolean flag `isEndOfWord` at each node to know if the path you've traveled actually forms a complete word, or is just a prefix.

steps: Insert 'cat': Root -> 'c' -> 'a' -> 't' (mark 't' as End).
Insert 'car': Root -> 'c' -> 'a' -> 'r' (mark 'r' as End). Notice they effortlessly share the 'c' -> 'a' branch!
Search 'cat': Follow 'c', follow 'a', follow 't'. Is 't' marked as End? Yes! Return true.

content.timeComplexity: O(L) where L is the length of the specific word.
content.spaceComplexity: O(N * L) where N is the number of words. However, sharing prefixes saves tremendous space!
commonMistakes: Forgetting to set `isEndOfWord = true` manually at the very end of the `insert` loop.
Confusing `search('cat')` (must end exactly at 't' with `isEndOfWord==true`) vs `startsWith('cat')` (just needs to reach 't', doesn't matter if it's the end).

interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Since we have many words that share the same starting letters, a Trie will drastically optimize our prefix matching from O(N*L) searching down to just O(L).'!
interviewTips.followUpPrep: How do you delete a word from a Trie without deleting shared prefixes?

relatedPatterns.description: A Trie is literally just an N-ary tree.

content.title: Graphs
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Graphs.
content.whatItIs: A pure Graph is like a roadmap. Unlike Trees (where data strictly flows top-down), Graph nodes (called vertices) can be connected to ANY other node, creating loops, cycles, and massive webs of data! Think of Facebook: You are a node, and your friends are nodes connected to you. There is no 'root' person.
whenToUse: When modeling real-world networks (Cities & Roads, Social Networks, the Internet).
When asked to find if two things are connected or grouped together.
When finding the shortest path (in terms of steps, not distance).
content.howItWorks: To represent a graph in code, we almost always use an 'Adjacency List' (a HashMap where the key is a node, and the value is a list of its neighbors). To traverse it, we use BFS (finding the shortest path via a Queue) or DFS (exploring deep via Recursion). BUT, because graphs can have loops, you MUST use a `visited` set to avoid running in circles forever!

exampleWalkthrough.input: nodes=[A,B,C], edges=[[A,B], [B,C]] - find if A is connected to C
steps: Build Adjacency List: A->[B], B->[A,C], C->[B].
Start DFS at A. Mark A visited. Neighbors of A is [B].
DFS at B. Mark B visited. Neighbors of B are [A, C]. A is visited, skip. Go to C.
DFS at C. Found target C! Return true.

content.timeComplexity: O(V + E) where V is vertices (nodes) and E is edges (connections).
content.spaceComplexity: O(V + E) to build the Adjacency List.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the `visited` HashSet. You WILL get an infinite loop.
Trying to build an Adjacency Matrix (a 2D Array) instead of an Adjacency List when the graph is sparse. It wastes huge amounts of memory.

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The input gives you `edges[][]` instead of an array. The prompt talks about 'islands', 'connections', 'components', or 'paths'.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Because this input models relationships that could contain cycles, I'll represent it using an Adjacency List and traverse it with a visited HashSet.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: Can you perform a Topological Sort?

relatedPatterns.description: The only way to guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

guide.hook: Graph = nodes + edges + a visited set. DFS to explore everything; BFS for the fewest steps.
guide.idea: A graph is things (nodes) joined by connections (edges); a grid is a graph where each cell links to its neighbours. Explore with DFS (go deep, a stack or recursion) or BFS (spread out in rings, a queue), always marking visited nodes. Ordering with dependencies is topological sort; 'are these connected?' as edges arrive is union-find.
guide.analogy: Exploring a cave system with a map you mark as you go. DFS follows one tunnel to its end before backing up; BFS explores every cave one step away, then two steps, and so on.
guide.breaks: In a cave you'd notice you've been somewhere. Code won't: without a visited set it loops forever around a cycle.

'Prerequisites', 'order of tasks', 'dependencies' → topological sort
'Is there a cycle?', 'is this a valid tree?', 'redundant connection' → union-find or DFS

medium.insight: Take courses with no remaining prerequisites first. If some courses never become ready, there's a cycle and it's impossible.
medium.code:
from collections import deque

def can_finish(num_courses, prerequisites):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indegree = [0] * num_courses
    for course, pre in prerequisites:
        adj[pre].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indegree[i] == 0)
    taken = 0
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for nxt in adj[c]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return taken == num_courses

mistakes: Marking a node visited when you pop it instead of when you push it, so it gets queued many times.
Going out of the grid: check 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols first.
In topological sort, forgetting that leftover nodes (not all taken) mean a cycle.
Forgetting the `visited` HashSet. You WILL get an infinite loop.
Trying to build an Adjacency Matrix (a 2D Array) instead of an Adjacency List when the graph is sparse. It wastes huge amounts of memory.

content.title: Advanced Graphs
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Advanced Graphs.
content.whatItIs: Advanced Graphs tackle problems where all paths are NOT created equal. Instead of just seeing if A connects to B, what if the road from A to B costs $10, but the road from A to C costs $5? Now we're dealing with *Weighted Cost* networks, *Directed* rules, or *Disjoint Sets*.
whenToUse: When finding the Absolute Cheapest/Shortest path in a Weighted Graph (Dijkstra's Algorithm).
When determining if a Directed Graph has a cycle (Course Schedule problems).
When grouping highly separate islands rapidly (Union-Find).
When finding the cheapest way to connect everything (Minimum Spanning Tree).
content.howItWorks:
There are 3 major magic spells here:
1. **Dijkstra's**: It's just BFS, but instead of a standard Queue, you use a PriorityQueue (Min-Heap) so it always explores the cheapest available path first!
2. **Topological Sort**: Used to determine the valid order of tasks when 'Task A' must be completed before 'Task B'.
3. **Union-Find**: An incredibly fast way to group components into separate 'sets' and check if two nodes belong to the same set.

steps: Start 0 cost 0. MinHeap=[(cost 0, Node 0)].
Pop 0. Neighbors: Node 1 cost 10, Node 2 cost 1. MinHeap=[(1, Node 2), (10, Node 1)].
Pop (1, Node 2). Neighbors: 2 gets to 1 for cost 2. Total cost = 1 (from 0->2) + 2 (from 2->1) = 3. Add to Heap. MinHeap=[(3, Node 1), (10, Node 1)].
Pop (3, Node 1). Reached Target 1! Total Cost is 3. (We completely ignored the expensive 10 cost path!)

content.timeComplexity: O(E log V) for Dijkstra's, nearly O(1) for Union Find path compression.
commonMistakes: Confusing Dijkstra's algorithm (Weighted Shortest Path) with standard BFS (Unweighted Shortest Path).
Forgetting to initialize the Parent array to `parent[i] = i` in a Union-Find object.

interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Because the edges have weights (or strict prerequisites), standard BFS is insufficient. I'll need to use Dijkstra's Algorithm (or Union-Find) to solve this optimally.'

guide.hook: Weighted edges? Dijkstra: always expand the cheapest known node next (a heap).
guide.idea: When edges have different costs, BFS isn't enough. Dijkstra uses a min-heap to always settle the cheapest unsettled node. Related tools: Bellman-Ford when there's a limit on the number of edges (or negative weights), Prim's or Kruskal's for the cheapest way to connect everything (minimum spanning tree), and topological sort for ordering.
guide.analogy: Water spreading from a source through pipes of different lengths. It reaches near places first, and the first time it reaches a place is via the shortest route.
guide.breaks: Water spreads everywhere at once; Dijkstra settles one node at a time. It also fails with negative edge costs, which water has no equivalent of.

'Connect all points with minimum total cost' → minimum spanning tree
'Order of letters / tasks from rules' → topological sort

content.title: 1-D Dynamic Programming
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for 1-D Dynamic Programming.
content.whatItIs: Dynamic Programming (DP) sounds terrifying, but it's actually just one simple idea: 'Don't do the same work twice!' Imagine I ask you to calculate 1+1+1+1. You say '4'. Then I add another '+1' to the end. Do you recount everything from the start? No! You just remember your last answer (4) and add 1 to get 5. That's exactly what DP is: saving the answers to smaller sub-problems exactly once so you can instantly lookup that answer later when solving a bigger problem.
whenToUse: When a problem asks for the 'minimum', 'maximum', 'longest', or 'total ways' to do something.
When you notice that a recursive solution calculates the exact same branches multiple times (Overlapping Subproblems).
content.howItWorks: There are two ways to do DP.\n1. **Top-Down (Memoization)**: You write a standard recursive function, but you add a HashMap or Array to 'cache' the result before returning. Next time the function is called with those same arguments, you return the cached result instantly.\n2. **Bottom-Up (Tabulation)**: You build an array (usually 1-Dimensional here) starting from index 0. You solve the smallest piece of the puzzle first, then use a `for-loop` to build up to the final answer.

exampleWalkthrough.input: Climbing Stairs: N=3 (can take 1 or 2 steps)
steps: Step 0 or 1: 1 way. dp=[1, 1].
Step 2: Can be reached from step 1 or step 0. So dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 2. dp=[1,1,2].
Step 3: Can be reached from step 2 or step 1. So dp[3] = dp[2] + dp[1] = 2+1 = 3. dp=[1,1,2,3].
Answer is dp[3], which is 3!

content.timeComplexity: O(N) because we only calculate each step exactly once.
content.spaceComplexity: O(N) to store the DP array. (Often optimizable to O(1) if you only need the last two values!)
commonMistakes: Forgetting to initialize the base cases properly before starting the `for` loop.
Using recursion without a cache, resulting in O(2^N) time limit exceeded errors.

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The problem talks about finding 'Max/Min/Longest', 'Number of ways', or involves jumping/taking steps.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Since this problem exhibits overlapping subproblems, a naive recursive approach will TLE. I will use Dynamic Programming to cache previous results.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: Can you optimize the space complexity from O(N) to O(1) by simply keeping track of the last two variables?

relatedPatterns.description: DP is just backtracking with a super-powered memory cache!

guide.hook: Write what dp[i] means in one sentence, then build it from dp[i − 1] and dp[i − 2].
guide.idea: Dynamic programming solves a problem by reusing answers to smaller versions of it. In 1-D, dp[i] is the answer for the first i items (or for amount i). Find the recurrence (how dp[i] comes from earlier entries), set the base cases, and fill the table in order.
guide.analogy: Climbing stairs and writing on each step how many ways there are to reach it. To fill in a new step, you just add the numbers on the one or two steps below — no recounting.
guide.breaks: On stairs the earlier numbers are obviously right. In DP you must define dp[i] precisely; if your definition is vague, the recurrence will quietly be wrong.
signals: 'Number of ways' to do something
'Minimum / maximum' cost, profit or count
Choices at each step that affect later choices (rob this house or not)
The brute-force recursion repeats the same sub-question many times

lookAlikes.clue: If one locally best choice can be wrong later (coins [1, 3, 4] for 6: greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1, DP gives 3 + 3), you need DP.
List all the ways → backtracking. Count them or find the best → DP.

guide.gutCheck: Would the brute force ask the same sub-question again and again? → DP.

flowchart LR
  A["dp[i − 2]"] --> C["dp[i]"]
  B["dp[i − 1]"] --> C
  C --> D["dp[i + 1]"]
diagram.caption: Each answer is built from the ones just before it, so every sub-question is solved exactly once.

guide.template:
def solve(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                 # dp[i] = answer using the first i items  <- write this down!
    dp[0] = ...                        # base case(s)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[i] = ...                    # from dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2], ...
    return dp[n]
guide.space: O(n), often O(1) by keeping the last two values
mistakes: Never writing down what dp[i] means.
Wrong base cases (dp[0] for climbing stairs is 1: one way to stand still).
In Coin Change, using 0 instead of infinity for 'impossible'.

content.title: 2-D Dynamic Programming
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for 2-D Dynamic Programming.
content.whatItIs: 2-D DP is the exact same concept as 1-D DP, but your 'state' depends on TWO variables instead of one. Imagine you are navigating a grid from the top-left to the bottom-right. The number of ways to reach a specific cell depends on the cell *above* it AND the cell to its *left*. Therefore, instead of a 1D array to remember answers, you need a full 2D array (a matrix)!
whenToUse: When dealing with grids or matrices (e.g., 'Unique Paths' or 'Longest Common Subsequence').
When the subproblem state requires tracking two distinct indices simultaneously (like taking items from Two different strings at the same time).
When dealing with classic Knapsack problems.
content.howItWorks: You create a `int[][] dp = new int[rows][cols]`. You carefully initialize the base cases—often the first row and the first column. Then, you use nested `for-loops` to iterate through every cell. For each cell, the answer is calculated by looking at the immediately neighboring cells that have ALREADY been computed (e.g., `dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]`).

exampleWalkthrough.input: grid 2x2. Find paths from 0,0 to 1,1. Right/Down only.
steps: Create 2x2 DP matrix.
Initialize first row to 1 (only 1 way to go straight right).
Initialize first col to 1 (only 1 way to go straight down).
Calculate cell (1,1). It's the sum of the cell above (1) and left (1). Thus dp[1][1] = 2.
Target cell is 2. Return 2!

content.timeComplexity: O(M * N) since you process every cell exactly once.
content.spaceComplexity: O(M * N) to store the DP grid (often optimizable to O(M) or O(N) by saving only the previous row).
commonMistakes: Messing up the matrix dimension sizes, resulting in `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
Filling the DP table in the wrong order so you accidentally try to query a cell that hasn't been computed yet!

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The problem literally gives you a 2D grid, asks you to compare TWO different strings, or presents a 'Knapsack' choice.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'Because our state depends on two varying constraints, I will build a 2D tabulation matrix to calculate the answers bottom-up.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: Can you optimize the space? (Hint: You usually only need to remember the *previous row*, not the entire matrix!)

content.title: Greedy
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Greedy.
content.whatItIs: A Greedy algorithm is like a person who always grabs the biggest piece of cake available RIGHT NOW, without thinking about tomorrow. At every single step, a Greedy algorithm makes the most optimal, locally 'best' choice possible, hoping that all these small optimal choices suddenly magically combine into the global best solution! It's much faster than Dynamic Programming because it refuses to look backward or reconsider.
whenToUse: When making a localized optimal choice guarantees a global optimal outcome (The Greedy Choice Property).
When the problem asks for the 'minimum', 'maximum', or 'longest' and involves jumping, intervals, or making a series of absolute choices.
content.howItWorks: Greedy algorithms don't have a strict universal template because the 'greedy choice' entirely depends on the problem. Usually, it involves **sorting** the data first (e.g., sorting by cost, or end time), and then looping through it once, greedily taking the best option at that exact moment while keeping a running tally.

exampleWalkthrough.input: Jump Game: nums = [2,3,1,1,4]. Can you reach the end?
steps: Set your 'Goal' to the absolute last index (index 4).
Look strictly at the index before it (Index 3). Can Index 3 jump to the Goal? (nums[3] = 1. 3+1 = 4. Yes!).
Greedy choice: Move the Goal post closer to index 3! We now only need to reach 3.
Index 2 can reach 3! Goal is now 2.
Index 1 can reach 2! Goal is now 1.
Index 0 can reach 1! Goal is now 0. We made it!

content.timeComplexity: O(N) (or O(N log N) if sorting is required first).
commonMistakes: Using Greedy when Dynamic Programming is required! Greedy only works if taking the *current best* choice doesn't ruin future choices. Often, a Greedy algorithm will fail complex edge cases that DP solves perfectly.
Forgetting to Sort the input data before making greedy decisions.

interviewTips.howToRecognize: The problem talks about 'Jumping max distance', 'Minimizing coin usage', or 'Scheduling the most activities'.
interviewTips.whatToSay: 'I noticed that making the locally optimal choice doesn't penalize future decisions. Therefore, I can bypass DP and use a strictly O(N) Greedy algorithm.'
interviewTips.followUpPrep: Can you prove why your Greedy choice doesn't fail? (Interviewer might ask you to justify why DP isn't needed).

content.title: Intervals
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Intervals.
content.whatItIs: An Interval is simply a start time and an end time (like a meeting from `[1:00 to 2:00]`). The 'Intervals' category of problems focuses entirely on giving you a massive list of these start/end times and asking you to find overlaps, merge them, or find free time. It's the exact logic used behind Google Calendar and hotel booking systems!
whenToUse: When the input is an array of pairs like `[[start1, end1], [start2, end2]]`.
When finding overlapping schedules, meeting rooms, or merging data ranges.
content.howItWorks: There is a universal 2-step trick to almost every Interval problem.\n1. **Sort the array:** You MUST sort the intervals by their `start` time. Without sorting, it's impossible to efficiently check overlaps.\n2. **Iterate and Merge:** After sorting, you simply loop through the intervals. If the `start` time of the *current* interval is strictly less than or equal to the `end` time of the *previous* interval, they overlap! You merge them by taking the `max()` of their end times.

steps: Sort by start: Already sorted [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10]].
Add [1,3] to our answer list.
Look at [2,6]. The start (2) is less than the previous end (3). OVERLAP! Merge them by taking max(3, 6). Answer list changes to [[1,6]].
Look at [8,10]. The start (8) is greater than previous end (6). No overlap. Just add it. Answer list: [[1,6], [8,10]]

content.timeComplexity: O(N log N) solely because of the initial sorting step.
content.spaceComplexity: O(N) to store the result list.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to sort the intervals first. The merging logic falls apart entirely if the input is `[[8,10], [1,3]]`.
Trying to merge arrays blindly without updating the reference pointer correctly in Java.

relatedPatterns.description: Merging intervals is actually a textbook Greedy approach: you optimally merge the current interval before moving on.

guide.idea: Interval problems almost always start by sorting. After sorting by start, two intervals overlap exactly when the next one starts before the last one ends. Then merge, count or remove as the problem asks.
guide.analogy: Putting meetings on a calendar in time order. You only need to compare each meeting with the one just before it to spot a clash.
guide.breaks: A calendar shows everything at a glance. In code, only the sort makes 'compare with the last one' enough; without it you'd have to compare every pair.

guide.template:
def rotate_clockwise(matrix):
    n = len(matrix)
    for i in range(n):                       # 1. transpose: swap across the diagonal
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i] = matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]
    for row in matrix:                       # 2. reverse each row
        row.reverse()
guide.time: Usually O(n²) for an n × n matrix, O(log n) for fast power

card.summary: Every number appears twice except one; find it with O(1) extra space.
card.clue: Pairs + one leftover + constant space.
card.trick: XOR everything; pairs cancel to 0.

card.summary: Count the 1 bits in an integer.
card.clue: 'Count the bits'.
card.trick: n & (n − 1) removes the lowest 1 bit; count how many times until n is 0.

card.summary: For every i from 0 to n, count the 1 bits in i.
card.clue: Bit counts for every number up to n, in O(n).
card.trick: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

card.summary: Reverse the 32 bits of an unsigned integer.
card.clue: Work on the binary form directly.
card.trick: 32 times: take n's last bit, shift the result left and add it, shift n right.

card.summary: Numbers 0 … n with one missing; find it.
card.clue: One missing value from a known complete range.
card.trick: XOR all indexes 0 … n and all values; everything present cancels out, leaving the missing one.

card.summary: Add two integers without using + or −.
card.technique: XOR for the sum, AND + shift for the carry
card.clue: 'Without + or −'.
card.trick: a ^ b adds without carrying; (a & b) << 1 is the carry; repeat until there's no carry (mask to 32 bits in Python).

card.summary: Reverse the digits of a 32-bit signed integer, returning 0 if it overflows.
card.technique: Digit popping with an overflow check
card.clue: Digits + a 32-bit limit.
card.trick: Pop the last digit with % 10 and push it onto the result × 10; check the limit before each push.

content.title: Bit Manipulation
content.introduction: Study guide and resource list for Bit Manipulation.
content.whatItIs: Deep down, computers don't understand 'Numbers' or 'Strings'. They solely understand 1s and 0s (voltage 'ON' and voltage 'OFF'). Bit Manipulation is the art of bypassing high-level code and directly hacking those raw binary digits! It is insanely fast and requires almost zero memory.
whenToUse: When asked to find a 'Single Number' in an array of duplicates.
When counting the number of '1' bits in an integer.
When reversing the binary representation of a number.
When doing highly-optimized sets and masks.
content.howItWorks:
You use special binary operators:
- `&` (AND): Returns 1 only if BOTH bits are 1.
- `|` (OR): Returns 1 if AT LEAST ONE bit is 1.
- `^` (XOR): Returns 1 if bits are DIFFERENT. (Crucial rule: `X ^ X = 0`).
- `<<` / `>>` (Shifts): literally slides all bits to the left or right, effectively multiplying/dividing by 2.

exampleWalkthrough.input: nums = [4,1,2,1,2]. Find the number that doesn't repeat.
steps: Start with 0.
0 XOR 4 = 4
4 XOR 1 = 5
5 XOR 2 = 7
7 XOR 1 = 6
Because X ^ X = 0, all the duplicate numbers perfectly canceled each other out! The only number left standing is 4.

commonMistakes: Confusing `&&` (Logical AND for booleans) with `&` (Bitwise AND for bits) in your if-statements.
Assuming bitwise operations are readable! They look like gibberish if you don't add comments.

relatedPatterns.description: Bit manipulation is just math performed in base-2.

guide.hook: XOR cancels pairs (a ^ a = 0), and x & (x − 1) deletes the lowest 1 bit.
guide.idea: Numbers are stored as bits, and bitwise operators work on all bits at once. A few facts solve most problems: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x; x & 1 is the last bit; x >> 1 drops the last bit; x & (x − 1) removes the lowest set bit.
guide.analogy: A row of light switches. XOR with a pattern flips those switches; flipping the same pattern twice puts everything back.
guide.breaks: Switches don't overflow. In Java or C, integers have a fixed number of bits and can overflow; Python integers grow, so problems like Sum of Two Integers need a mask in Python.

'Count the 1 bits', 'reverse the bits'
'Without using + or −'
'Missing number' in 0…n (XOR or the sum formula)

lookAlikes.clue: A hash set also finds the single number, but with O(n) memory; XOR does it with O(1).
Missing Number can also use n(n + 1)/2 − sum; XOR avoids any overflow worry.

guide.gutCheck: Pairs cancelling, single bits, or 'no + allowed'? → bits.

diagram.caption: XOR can be reordered, and each pair cancels to 0, leaving only the number without a partner.

guide.template:
def bit_tricks(x):
    last_bit = x & 1               # 1 if x is odd
    x_without_last = x >> 1        # drop the last bit (x // 2)
    lowest_removed = x & (x - 1)   # remove the lowest 1 bit
    count = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1                 # one loop per 1 bit
        count += 1
    return last_bit, x_without_last, lowest_removed, count

def single(nums):
    acc = 0
    for x in nums:
        acc ^= x                   # pairs cancel: a ^ a = 0
    return acc

Forgetting operator precedence: write (x & 1) == 1, with brackets.
